questions.q: What makes this lesson's az vm create / run-instances commands different in intent from the earlier Azure and AWS compute lessons?
options: They deploy explicitly into the VNet/subnet/NSG or VPC/subnet/security group Chapter 2 already built, instead of teaching the flags in isolation
They use entirely different, previously uncovered flags
They no longer require an image or instance size to be specified
They disable the platform's billing for the instance
questions.explain: The mechanics are the same ones taught earlier; what's new here is launching with intent into the specific network Chapter 2 built and Lesson 8 verified.

questions.q: What do --vnet-name and --subnet do in this lesson's az vm create example?
options: Place the VM's NIC inside the named VNet and subnet instead of a default Azure would otherwise create
Change the VM's operating system image
Attach a public IP address automatically
Have no effect unless --nsg is also omitted
questions.explain: Naming the VNet and subnet explicitly puts the VM on the exact network Chapter 2 built, not a new default VNet.

questions.q: Why does the Azure example include --public-ip-address ""?
options: To stop Azure from automatically provisioning a public IP, appropriate for a private application-tier subnet
To assign a specific static public IP address
Because az vm create requires this flag on every call
To disable the VM's network interface entirely
questions.explain: An empty string overrides az vm create's default behavior of provisioning a public IP, which is wrong for a private subnet.

questions.q: What happens if --subnet-id is omitted from an aws ec2 run-instances call?
options: AWS silently launches the instance into the account's default VPC and default subnet
The run-instances call fails immediately with an error
AWS prompts interactively for a subnet before launching
The instance launches with no network interface at all
questions.explain: Without --subnet-id, AWS substitutes the default VPC's default subnet rather than failing the launch.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what's the real risk of letting Azure or AWS substitute a default network at launch?
options: The instance boots successfully but sits on a network nobody designed, with none of Chapter 2's NSG or security group rules applied — a gap usually found later, at a worse time
The instance fails to boot, so the problem is caught immediately
There is no real risk, since defaults are always secure
The instance automatically inherits Chapter 2's NSG rules regardless of which network it lands on
questions.explain: The instance runs fine on the surface, which is exactly why this gap tends to surface later as an unreachable or unexpectedly open instance.
